content.title: About
content.content: Bran flakes are a whole‑grain breakfast cereal made from wheat bran. They have a neutral taste, a crunchy texture, and are commonly enjoyed with milk, yogurt, or fruit.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bran is the outer layer of the grain, rich in fiber and nutrients.
Bran flakes are popular in diet plans because of their low calorie density.
Unlike sweet cereals, they contain no added sugar.
Bran can help improve digestion and regulate blood sugar levels.
In some regions they are simply called "bran flakes" or "wheat bran flakes".

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Both soluble and insoluble fiber support gut health and promote satiety.

items.title: Low sugar content
items.content: The absence of added sugars makes them suitable for blood‑glucose management.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Bran provides thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Iron, magnesium and zinc in bran contribute to blood formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Fiber helps lower LDL cholesterol, reducing cardiovascular risk.

items.title: Gluten sensitivity
items.content: Bran flakes contain gluten and should be avoided by people with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Excess fiber
items.content: Large servings may cause bloating, gas, or diarrhea in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals when consumed in very high amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Typically pour milk or a plant‑based beverage over the flakes, add fresh or dried fruit, nuts, honey, or yogurt. They can also be used as a base for granola bars or incorporated into baked goods.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed container in a cool, dry place. For extended shelf life, store in the refrigerator to prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: A hamburger is a classic fast‑food item consisting of a medium beef patty placed between a soft wheat bun. It is often served with lettuce, tomato, onion, cheese, sauces, and pickles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first hamburger was served in the United States in the late 19th century.
The name “hamburger” comes from the German city of Hamburg, where similar meat patties were popular.
Hamburgers gained massive popularity among American soldiers during World War II.
There are more than 300 hamburger variations, including vegetarian and vegan versions.
The world’s largest hamburger weighed over 1 ton.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The beef patty provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Hamburgers supply B12, B6, and niacin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc is important for immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of protein, fat, and carbohydrates provides quick energy.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Excessive intake may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Salt and sauces
items.content: Large amounts of salt and sauces can increase the risk of hypertension.

items.title: Caloric content
items.content: Hamburgers are calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: The bun contains gluten, and toppings may include dairy, which is relevant for people with allergies.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hamburgers are typically eaten by hand, holding them with both hands. You can add fresh vegetables, cheese, avocado, or swap heavy sauces for lighter options.

content.title: Storage
content.content: A prepared hamburger can be kept in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. The patty can be frozen for up to 3 months, and the bun should be stored in a dry place protected from moisture.

potato-boiled-from-fresh-peel-eaten-made.title: Boiled Potato, fresh, peel eaten, with butter

content.title: About
content.content: Boiled potato is a dish made from fresh potatoes cooked in water until tender, with the skin left on and eaten. It is commonly finished with a pat of butter, which adds a smooth, rich flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes are one of the world’s most widely consumed foods, grown in over 125 countries.
Eating the skin boosts fiber, vitamin, and mineral intake.
Butter added to boiled potatoes enhances absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).
Boiled potatoes feature in traditional dishes worldwide, from Russian potato pancakes to Spanish papas a la brava.
When stored properly, boiled potatoes keep in the fridge for up to 5 days.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Boiled potatoes provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Good source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: The skin supplies fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Plain boiled potatoes contain virtually no fat; a modest amount of butter keeps the dish low‑calorie.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Boiled potatoes can raise blood sugar quickly, which may be a concern for people with diabetes.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: Although rare, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to potatoes.

items.title: Solanine content
items.content: Green spots or sprouting indicate solanine, a toxic compound; such parts should be removed.

items.title: Excess butter
items.content: Butter adds saturated fat and calories; use it in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot boiled potatoes with a pat of butter on top. They can be eaten plain, added to salads, used in casseroles, or mashed.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep boiled potatoes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags.

content.title: About
content.content: Quinoa is the seed of the Chenopodium quinoa plant native to the Andes. The “fat added” version is pre‑toasted quinoa enriched with vegetable oils, which raises its energy density and gives a richer flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Quinoa is a pseudocereal, not a true grain, but nutritionally it is often compared to rice and couscous.
The fat content is boosted to about 8 % by adding olive and sunflower oils.
Quinoa contains all nine essential amino acids, making it a complete plant protein source.
In ancient Andean cultures quinoa was called the “mother of all grains” and used in ceremonial dishes.
Toasting and adding fat shortens cooking time: the product is ready in 5‑7 minutes.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: One serving (≈ 185 g) provides about 8 g of plant protein, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Added monounsaturated fats (olive oil) help lower LDL cholesterol levels.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Quinoa supplies both soluble and insoluble fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Abundant micronutrients
items.content: It contains magnesium, iron, zinc, phosphorus and B‑vitamins, essential for metabolism.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Quinoa raises blood sugar slowly, which is beneficial for diabetes management and weight control.

items.title: Pseudocereal allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to quinoa.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Added fats increase the energy value to ≈ 210 kcal/100 g, so portion size should be monitored.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Quinoa contains oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fat‑added quinoa works well as a side dish, in salads, soups, or vegetarian patties. Rinse it first, then simmer in water (1 : 2 ratio) for 5‑7 minutes until tender.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in an airtight container. For longer shelf life keep it refrigerated to prevent oxidation of the added oils.

soft-drink-pepper-type-decaffeinated-die.title: Soft drink, pepper type, decaffeinated, diet

content.title: About
content.content: A carbonated soft drink flavored with pepper, free of caffeine and sugar. It consists of sparkling water infused with natural pepper extract and non‑caloric sweeteners. The product is aimed at consumers who want a refreshing, slightly spicy taste without calories.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pepper‑flavored sodas first appeared in Japan in the early 2000s as an alternative to fruit flavors.
Decaffeinated versions allow enjoyment by people sensitive to caffeine.
The diet sweeteners used are approved by EU and US food safety authorities.
Carbonation enhances the perception of pepper aroma by releasing volatile compounds.
Pepper contains capsaicin, which may modestly boost metabolism.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Capsaicin from pepper can slightly increase thermogenesis, helping calorie burning.

items.title: Zero calories
items.content: The sugar‑free, caffeine‑free formula adds no calories, useful for weight management.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Sparkling water contributes to daily fluid intake.

items.title: Caffeine‑free
items.content: Suitable for individuals avoiding stimulants, including pregnant women and children.

items.title: Antioxidant potential
items.content: Pepper extract provides small amounts of vitamin C and polyphenols.

items.title: Sensitivity to spiciness
items.content: Some people may experience throat or stomach irritation from the pepper flavor.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Certain consumers may have discomfort from sucralose or acesulfame‑K.

items.title: Carbonation
items.content: Excessive intake of carbonated drinks can cause bloating.

items.title: Pepper allergy
items.content: Rare allergic reactions to pepper extract are possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve chilled, optionally over ice or with a slice of lemon to enhance freshness. Ideal as a refreshing snack between meals or after workouts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 5‑7 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Tomato and cucumber salad is made from fresh tomatoes, cucumbers, vegetable oil and vinegar. It is a light, refreshing dish popular in summer, low in calories and easy to prepare.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that supports heart health.
Cucumbers are composed of more than 95% water, making them an excellent source of hydration.
The combination of vinegar and oil enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins from the vegetables.
In Russian cuisine the classic “Olivier” salad often includes tomatoes, but here they are the star ingredient.
The salad can be served as a standalone dish or as a side to meat and fish.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Both tomatoes and cucumbers provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: High water content and low fat make this salad suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from the vegetables promotes healthy bowel function and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene and other phytochemicals in tomatoes protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Cucumbers help maintain the body’s fluid balance due to their high water content.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes, such as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: A large amount of vinegar can increase stomach acidity and cause discomfort for people with gastritis.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: If the vegetables are not organic, they may contain pesticide residues; thorough washing is recommended before consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled, tossing the sliced vegetables with a mixture of oil and vinegar. Add fresh herbs, spices, or a pinch of salt to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, keep the dressing separate to prevent the vegetables from becoming soggy.
